newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW - Telstra says Telecom NZ feeling the heat.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Telstra says Telecom NZ feeling the heat.

text.p: Telstra New Zealand managing director Peter Williamson on Tuesday hailed Telecom New Zealand Limited's latest annual result as a victory for competition and for the customer.
Australian-owned Telstra is one of Telecom's latest rivals in the New Zealand market.
"I can understand them (Telecom) being disappointed because profits are down from what they're accustomed to," Williamson told Reuters.

"But from New Zealand's point of view, it looked like the first time in a supposed free-wheeling economy where the customer is actually starting to see some benefit from competition," he said in a telephone interview.
Telecom last week reported an 18.9 percent slide in annual profit to NZ$581.4 million from $716.8 million a year earlier.
Telecom said the slowing New Zealand economy had impacted on earnings, but Williamson said Telstra had not experienced any evidence of an economic slowdown.
"No evidence here, no evidence of the economy slowing," he said. "New Zealand continues to be a reasonably healthy economy from my perspective."
Rather, Telecom's profit result indicated that competition was eating away at its revenues, he argued.

"What it was saying was things like some of Telecom's key revenue streams, because of competition, were starting to come down...and that less of the profit out of the telcommunications industry was leaving New Zealand," Williamson said.
"When you understand that about 82 percent of Telecom's profit goes offshore, it (the result) is a good thing for New Zealand."

Williamson said Telstra, the Australian state-owned telephone utility which became fully operational in New Zealand in December 1995, was now a well established niche player here and was putting pressure on its rivals.
"Connections for us last month were up 65 percent," he said.
"We're billing pretty much in excess of NZ$2 million a month from a standing start of $70,000 18 months ago."

He said Telstra NZ would become cash and EBIT positive within the next seven to eight months. It was also on target to achieve a 10 percent share of the New Zealand market within three years of launch, and about 20 percent in five years.

While the company had not managed to get its planned cellular service up and running on schedule, a mobile product was likely to be available by Christmas this year and business targets for 1997/98 would be met.
"We're in a very, very good position. We would say our targets for 1997/98 are assured because of the business we've written," Williamson said.
Targets included increasing billings by around 300 percent. "And we're already starting to launch our trans-Tasman ISDN."
Telstra was wary of making the same mistakes in New Zealand that Telecom had made in Australia with its subsidiary Pacific Star, which is in the process of being divested.
"We don't want to be like Pac Star and discount ourselves out of business. You've got to be prudent," Williamson said.
"So we've not tried to rape the markets. You haven't seen us in any price wars. We just go about our business."
